summary.text: A finite check shows that for every \(1\le d\le2025\), there are primes \(p,q\) with different final digits and \(pq\le150\) such that neither divides \(d\). Since \(d\) is invertible modulo \(pq\), some \(i<pq\) satisfies \(pq\mid a+id\), so one of the first 150 terms has prime divisors with different final digits, a contradiction.

full_proof.text:
Call a positive integer lopsided if all of its prime divisors have the same final decimal digit. We prove that there cannot be an arithmetic progression
\[
 a,a+d,a+2d,\ldots,a+149d
\]
with \(a\ge 2\), \(1\le d\le 2025\), all of whose terms are lopsided.

We first establish a finite lemma about the possible common difference.

Consider the following pairs of primes:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(2,3),(2,5),(2,7),(2,11),(2,13),(2,17),\\
&(3,5),(3,7),(3,11),(3,17),\\
&(5,7),(5,11),(5,13),(5,17),\\
&(7,11),(7,13),(11,13).
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}
\]
In every pair the two primes have different final decimal digits. Their products, in the same grouping, are
\[
\begin{aligned}
&6,10,14,22,26,34,\\
&15,21,33,51,\\
&35,55,65,85,\\
&77,91,143,
\end{aligned}
\]
so every product is at most \(150\).

We claim that for every integer \(d\) with \(1\le d\le 2025\), at least one pair \((p,q)\) in (1) has the property that neither \(p\) nor \(q\) divides \(d\).

Suppose, to the contrary, that this fails for some such \(d\). Then every pair in (1) is “hit” by a prime divisor of \(d\): for every listed pair \((p,q)\), at least one of \(p,q\) divides \(d\).

Among the five primes
\[
2,3,5,7,11,
\]
every pair occurs in (1). Consequently at most one of these five primes can fail to divide \(d\); if two failed to divide \(d\), their pair would not be hit. We split according to the possible omitted prime.

* If none is omitted, then
  \[
  2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11=2310
  \]
  divides \(d\). Since \(d>0\), this gives \(d\ge2310>2025\), a contradiction.

* Suppose \(11\nmid d\). The other four primes \(2,3,5,7\) divide \(d\). The listed pair \((11,13)\) must be hit, so \(13\mid d\). Hence
  \[
  2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot13=2730
  \]
  divides \(d\), again making \(d>2025\).

* Suppose \(7\nmid d\). Then \(2,3,5,11\) divide \(d\). The pair \((7,13)\) forces \(13\mid d\). Thus
  \[
  2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot11\cdot13=4290
  \]
  divides \(d\), which is impossible for \(d\le2025\).

* Suppose \(5\nmid d\). Then \(2,3,7,11\) divide \(d\). The pairs \((5,13)\) and \((5,17)\) force both \(13\mid d\) and \(17\mid d\). In particular, \(d\) is divisible by
  \[
  2\cdot3\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13\cdot17=102102>2025,
  \]
  again a contradiction.

* Suppose \(3\nmid d\). Then \(2,5,7,11\) divide \(d\). The pair \((3,17)\) forces \(17\mid d\), so
  \[
  2\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot17=13090
  \]
  divides \(d\), which is impossible.

* Finally, suppose \(2\nmid d\). Then \(3,5,7,11\) divide \(d\). The pairs \((2,13)\) and \((2,17)\) force both \(13\mid d\) and \(17\mid d\). Therefore
  \[
  3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13\cdot17=255255
  \]
  divides \(d\), also impossible.

These cases exhaust the possibilities, proving the claim: for every \(1\le d\le2025\), there are primes \(p,q\) from one of the pairs in (1) such that
\[
p\nmid d,\qquad q\nmid d,
\tag{2}
\]
with
\[
p\bmod 10\ne q\bmod 10
\quad\text{and}\quad
pq\le150.
\tag{3}
\]

Now suppose for contradiction that \(a\ge2\), \(1\le d\le2025\), and all the \(150\) numbers \(a+id\), \(0\le i<150\), are lopsided. Choose \(p,q\) as in the preceding claim.

Because \(p\) and \(q\) have different final digits, they are distinct primes. Since neither divides \(d\), primality gives
\[
\gcd(d,p)=\gcd(d,q)=1.
\]
As \(p\) and \(q\) are distinct, it follows that
\[
\gcd(d,pq)=1.
\]
Thus \(d\) is invertible modulo \(pq\). The congruence
\[
id\equiv -a\pmod{pq}
\tag{4}
\]
therefore has a solution modulo \(pq\): explicitly, its solution class is
\[
i\equiv -a d^{-1}\pmod{pq}.
\]
Choose the least nonnegative representative \(i\) of this class. Then
\[
0\le i<pq\le150,
\]
so \(0\le i<150\). Hence \(a+id\) is one of the assumed \(150\) terms of the progression.

Congruence (4) says
\[
a+id\equiv0\pmod{pq}.
\]
Consequently \(pq\mid a+id\), and therefore both \(p\mid a+id\) and \(q\mid a+id\). Also \(a+id\ge a\ge2\), so this term is a positive integer and \(p,q\) genuinely occur among its prime divisors. But by (3), \(p\) and \(q\) have different final decimal digits. Thus the prime divisors of \(a+id\) do not all have the same final digit, meaning that \(a+id\) is not lopsided.

This contradicts the assumption that every one of the \(150\) terms is lopsided. Therefore there are no integers \(a\ge2\) and \(1\le d\le2025\) for which all of
\[
a,a+d,\ldots,a+149d
\]
occur in A381159. Hence the conjectured arithmetic progression does not exist.
